19.5 Reactivity of Carbonyl Group

Ketones and aldehydes undergo many reactions to give a wide variety of useful derivatives. Their most common reactions are nucleophilic addition; addition of a nucleophile and a proton across the C=O double bond. The reactivity of the carbonyl group arises from the high electronegativity of the oxygen atom and the resulting polarization of the carbon-oxygen double bond. The electrophilic carbonyl carbon atom is sp²-hybridized and planar, and relatively unhindered (compare to tetrahedral carbon) and is more susceptible for attack by a nucleophile, from either side of the double bond. When a nucleophile attacks the carbonyl group, the carbon atom changes hybridization from sp² to sp³, with corresponding change in geometry from trigonal planar to tetrahedral as shown below.

19.6 Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones

Aldehydes and ketones are very reactive substances mostly undergoing nucleophilic addition reaction across C=O bond. These can also be oxidized as well as reduced. Some of their reactions are;

19.6.1 Nucleophilic Addition reactions: (Acid and Base catalyzed)

As already discussed in Section 19.5, that aldehydes and ketones mainly undergo nucleophilic additions reactions. In nucleophilic addition reaction, the nucleophile attacks on the carbonyl carbon, and the hybridization of carbon changes from sp² to sp³. The geometry also changes from trigonal planar to tetrahedral. The electrons of the pi bond are forced out to the oxygen atom to form an alkoxide ion, which is protonated to give the product of nucleophilic addition. A generalized example of nucleophilic addition of a strong nucleophile (N̈u⁻), followed by protonation of alkoxide ion is shown below.

These reactions may be either acid catalyzed or base catalyzed.

a. Acid–Catalyzed Addition Reactions

Because of the unshared electron pair on oxygen atom, carbonyl oxygen acts as Lewis base, and can be protonated. Acid can catalyze the addition of weak nucleophiles to carbonyl compounds by protonating the carbonyl oxygen atom, to form an oxonium ion. This increases the electrophilic nature of the carbonyl carbon by inducing more positive charge on it and thus enhances its ability to be attacked by weak nucleophiles. For example, the mechanism of acid-catalyzed nucleophilic addition of generalized reaction is given below.

Addition of water, alcohol, ammonia, amines etc. generally follow this mechanism.

b. Base-Catalyzed Addition Reactions

A base-catalyzed nucleophilic addition will take place in the presence of a strong base, which is usually the conjugate base of a reagent used for nucleophilic addition. The base which is also a nucleophile, attacks at the carbon atom of the carbon–oxygen double bond, and pi electrons of C=O bond move to the oxygen atom, which can easily accommodate the negative charge, because of its high electronegativity. The reaction is completed by the abstraction of a proton, from the reagent by negative oxygen, to regenerate the base. Thus, base increases the nucleophilic character of the reagent to be added.
